**My Reasoning**

I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. My father grew wheat and corn here, and so did his father. The land is flat, the soil is decent — sandy loam, not too deep — and I have access to the village well for irrigation. I have about 8 mu of contracted land.

In Quzhou, there's really only one thing that makes sense: winter wheat followed by summer corn. That's what everyone does, that's what the government extension station recommends, and that's what earns money at the grain station. I'm not going to try cotton or vegetables — I don't have the connections to sell them, and I'm getting older. Keep it simple.

For wheat, I'll use the Jimai variety the seed shop sells — it's improved, gives better yield than the old seed, doesn't cost too much. I'll apply base fertilizer before planting: diammonium phosphate and urea mixed in. I always irrigate at jointing and heading — that's when the wheat needs water most. My father taught me that. I'll spray herbicide in spring when the weeds come up, then a fungicide near heading for powdery mildew, which is bad here.

After wheat harvest in June, I'll plant hybrid corn right away — no time to waste. I'll skip deep plowing to save fuel money and just use the rotary machine or direct seed. Corn doesn't need much — I'll top-dress nitrogen at the 6-leaf stage. I usually irrigate once if August is dry.

I don't like using too many chemicals, but I do what the neighbors do. Nobody in the village does soil tests. I just apply what I applied last year — it worked before, it'll work again.
